title: Biggest and smallest together
idea: TOOL: compare max and min directly; pick the right one from the wording. ~30% review of max.

exercises.prompt: 'What was the lowest price?' Which tool?
exercises.explanation: 'Lowest' points to the single smallest value — min.

exercises.prompt: 'What was the highest price?' Which tool?
exercises.explanation: 'Highest' points to the single biggest value — max. Same pattern, flipped comparison.

exercises.prompt: Match each goal to its comparison sign.
exercises.explanation: Max uses >, min uses <, and both start best at the first value. One pattern, two jobs.
Two best-so-far trackers in one loop: big climbs to 9, low drops to 2. You can find both at once.

exercises.prompt: You can track the biggest and the smallest in the same loop using two best-so-far variables.
exercises.explanation: Each has its own variable and its own if. One pass, two answers — because both are the same pattern.

exercises.prompt: Which statements about the max/min pair are true? (pick all)
options: Both start best at the first value
Min needs a completely different loop
exercises.explanation: Min and max are the same loop; only > vs < differs; both start at the first value. They are not different loops.
42 is the biggest — the max loop from last unit.
8 is the smallest — same list, flipped comparison.

exercises.prompt: 'The range is biggest minus smallest.' How many best-so-far loops answer 'what is the range?'
options: Two kinds of tracking — a max and a min
exercises.explanation: Range needs both the biggest and the smallest, so you track both (one loop with two variables works).

exercises.prompt: Why is learning min easy right after max?
options: It is the same pattern with the comparison flipped — you transfer what you already know
It is a totally new idea
exercises.explanation: Pattern transfer: once you own the best-so-far loop, flipping > to < gives you min for free.
